entities.summary:
Tolmides, son of Tolmaeus, was a preeminent Athenian general whose military prowess and strategic vision significantly expanded and consolidated Athenian power during the mid-5th century BCE, particularly in the lead-up to and during the First Peloponnesian War. Operating between approximately 458 and 446 BCE, Tolmides stood alongside figures like Pericles and Myronides in shaping Athens' thalassocracy, or naval empire, across the Aegean and into the Corinthian Gulf. His campaigns were instrumental in projecting Athenian influence, securing maritime routes, and establishing a network of cleruchies that simultaneously strengthened the Athenian citizenry and provided strategic outposts against rival powers, primarily Sparta and its allies.

His most celebrated achievement was the circumnavigation of the Peloponnese in 455 BCE, a daring naval expedition that showcased Athenian naval supremacy. During this campaign, Tolmides captured the Spartan arsenal at Gythium, ravaged the Laconian coast, and, most significantly, seized the strategic city of Naupactus in the Corinthian Gulf. He subsequently settled Messenian Helots, refugees from the Third Messenian War, at Naupactus, creating a loyal Athenian outpost that would prove invaluable in future conflicts. Tolmides further solidified Athenian control by establishing cleruchies on Euboea, Naxos, and other islands, transforming these territories into extensions of Athenian power and providing land for landless Athenian citizens, thus bolstering both military strength and democratic stability.
